title: Double Dose of Speedrun | Sicilian, Scandi | 800 Elo | Top Theory Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: e4, the knight to f6, and White throws the queen out to h5 — a famous early sortie. We answer with c5, striking at the centre and offering the pawn.
The queen takes c5. Obviously
the knight grabs on e4 — we've traded our c-pawn for his e-pawn, but the real point is that White has developed nothing but his queen.
Where White puts the queen matters — if it dropped back to e3 we'd hit it with d5. He keeps it on h5, and the knight to c6 and later b5 are our ideas.
We develop with the knight to c6. You might ask, what if White chases it with d3? So be it — the knight just goes back; we've lost nothing by developing.
The bishop to c4, obviously threatening mate on f7, so we have to be careful — don't play d6, which doesn't defend the f7-pawn.
There are two good moves here; the one more consistent with our strategy is e6, which blunts the bishop.
If I were White I'd continue with the knight to c3 or c3. There's a clear drawback to e6 —
— but it's true in many positions that it's fine to tuck a piece back to d7 temporarily; it won't change the assessment. We play d5, striking at the bishop and grabbing the centre.
The bishop to b5, and we develop the bishop to c5. We break the pin naturally, so we don't really need the bishop to d7 or a6 — we can just keep developing.
Is the queen to b6 ever an idea? Generally yes, it's a good move in many positions, especially here — but
castling is more flexible right now: we keep our options open and unpin the knight.
And remember the queen to b6 would threaten the bishop, but White's f2-pawn is well defended, so that's not the whole story.
The knight to d4 — the queen drops back, we take his bishop, but then he takes our knight; what do we actually gain? Let me think it through.
The knight to d4 might even be the more accurate try — I'm not certain; the queen to a5 was a perfectly legitimate alternative that worked much the same. He plays the knight to a3.

The knight takes f3 with check. These opponents do find good moves — the bishop to c4, the queen back to f3, the bishop to b5, and the knight to h3 was the only move defending the pawn — but then it falls apart anyway.
We won't have to wait long to cross a thousand, and then we'll get more serious games; this one was won a little early.
Let's replay it from the top and look closer at the queen sortie.

The queen takes c5, the knight takes — I forget exactly how the well-known game went; I believe the stronger side also took on c5.

The knight takes e4, the queen to h5 — of course this is total garbage; Black is already clearly better, and White has to be accurate just to
avoid being basically lost. The knight to c5, the queen to g5, the knight to e4, the queen to c5 — the queen just shuffles while we develop for free.
There's an old line about missing a good opportunity to resign — that applies here for White.
So anyway — the queen to h5, we play the knight to c6, continuing our development,
and the bishop to c4 threatens checkmate in one. This is a pattern you should identify instantly, even as a beginner:
the queen from f3 or h5 attacks f7, and so does the bishop — so we just play e6, and it's really the main thing to know.
It's not the end of the world that the light-squared bishop is somewhat confined by the pawns.

natural. The bishop to c5, then we castle, we

d4. What would we have done if White had
dropped the queen back to d1? There are two options here.
The easy option is just the knight takes b5, and after d-takes-e4 we recapture d-takes-e4, and
we're up a pawn with better development and the two bishops; his knight is
crappy on h3 — Black is much better. The queens can be traded, but that doesn't change the nature of the position: Black is
winning here. The second option, a bit more convoluted, is to note that two pieces are hanging at once — the knight and the bishop —
and since you're already losing the knight on e4, you might as well give it away for the maximum material. Once you phrase it that way,
this move also attacks the queen, so it's almost a check — you force White to take, then you take the bishop, and you shatter
White's kingside. He can still castle, but
then we can play e5, occupying the centre; the bishop is strong and the other bishop is good as well — this is a great position for Black.
The queen to h4 is also good — it's just really, really bad for White.
But obviously the knight to a3 and the knight to f3 is
just game over. The knight to a3, the knight takes f3 with check — and I'll probably combine this with another speedrun game.
